content: The text provided appears to be a detailed reference list and summary of guidelines, studies, and recommendations related to maternal and neonatal health, particularly focusing on the prevention of early-onset Group B Streptococcus (GBS) disease in newborns. 1. A systematic review and meta-analysis published in BJOG in 2020 evaluated the effectiveness of intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis (IAP) during childbirth to prevent early-onset Group B Streptococcal (GBS) disease in newborns. The study synthesized evidence to guide clinical practice in reducing neonatal infections caused by GBS. 2. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a global strategy to address antimicrobial resistance, emphasizing the importance of judicious antibiotic use to prevent the emergence of resistant pathogens. This strategy is accessible through WHO's official publications. 3. A birth cohort study by Li et al., published in Annals of Clinical Microbiology and Antimicrobials in 2022, demonstrated that early-life exposure to antibiotics is associated with an increased risk of childhood overweight and obesity. This relationship is mediated by dysbiosis of the gut microbiota, highlighting the long-term consequences of antibiotic use in infancy. 4. Zhang et al. conducted a meta-analysis, published in the World Allergy Organization Journal in 2021, which found a significant association between infant antibiotic exposure and an increased risk of developing childhood asthma. This underscores the need for cautious antibiotic prescribing practices in early life. 5. Vogel et al., in a 2019 article in BMJ Global Health, described the development and application of a living guidelines approach for WHO recommendations on maternal and perinatal health. This approach ensures that guidelines remain up-to-date with the latest evidence and are responsive to emerging health priorities. 6. The WHO has identified priority questions for maternal and perinatal health recommendations for 2024–2025. These questions aim to address critical gaps in evidence and improve outcomes for mothers and newborns globally. 7. The WHO Handbook for Guideline Development (Second Edition) provides a comprehensive framework for creating evidence-based recommendations. This resource ensures methodological rigor and transparency in the development of health guidelines. 8. A systematic review and meta-analysis by Panneflek et al., published in eClinicalMedicine in 2024, compared various strategies for intrapartum antibiotic prophylaxis to prevent GBS infections in newborns. The study evaluated the effectiveness of different screening and treatment protocols. 9. Constantinou et al. synthesized evidence on the values, preferences, and perspectives of parents and healthcare providers regarding the acceptability, feasibility, equity, and outcomes of screening strategies to prevent early-onset GBS disease in newborns. This preprint highlights the importance of stakeholder engagement in guideline development. 10. Downe et al., in a 2016 systematic scoping review published in BJOG, identified the processes and outcomes of antenatal care that are most important to healthy pregnant women. Their findings emphasize the need for patient-centered care in maternity services. 11. In a 2018 systematic qualitative review published in PLOS ONE, Downe et al. explored what matters most to women during childbirth. The study highlighted the importance of respectful, individualized care and positive birth experiences. 12. Alonso-Coello et al., in a 2016 article in BMJ, introduced the GRADE Evidence to Decision (EtD) frameworks. These frameworks provide a systematic and transparent approach to making well-informed healthcare decisions, ensuring that recommendations are based on the best available evidence. 13. Lewin et al., in a 2018 article in Implementation Science, described the application of GRADE-CERQual to qualitative evidence synthesis findings. This methodology enhances the confidence in qualitative evidence used to inform healthcare decisions. 14. Evers et al., in a 2005 article in the International Journal of Technology Assessment in Health Care, proposed a consensus-based criteria list for assessing the methodological quality of economic evaluations. This tool, known as the Consensus on Health Economic Criteria (CHEC), is widely used in health economics research. 15. The WHO has published guidelines on the core components of infection prevention and control programs at the national and acute healthcare facility levels. These guidelines aim to reduce healthcare-associated infections and improve patient safety. 16. The WHO Model List of Essential Medicines (23rd edition, 2023) outlines the selection and use of essential medicines to address priority health needs. This list is a critical resource for ensuring equitable access to effective treatments. 17. A systematic review by Odubamowo et al., published in the European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology in 2023, compared self-collected versus healthcare professional-collected swabs for identifying vaginal-rectal colonization with GBS in late pregnancy. The findings inform best practices for GBS screening. 18. The WHO has released updated recommendations for managing common childhood conditions, including newborn infections, dysentery, pneumonia, and severe acute malnutrition. These recommendations are based on the latest evidence to improve child health outcomes. 19. The WHO guideline on managing possible serious bacterial infections in young infants when referral is not feasible provides practical recommendations for healthcare providers in resource-limited settings. This guideline addresses critical gaps in neonatal care. 20. The WHO standards for improving the quality of maternal and newborn care in health facilities emphasize the importance of evidence-based practices, respectful care, and effective health system interventions to reduce maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality. 21. The WHO has conducted a full value of vaccine assessment for a Group B Streptococcus vaccine. This assessment evaluates the potential impact of a GBS vaccine on reducing neonatal infections and improving maternal and child health outcomes. 22. The WHO Guideline Development Group (GDG) and Evidence Synthesis Group (ESG) include experts from diverse fields who contribute to the development of evidence-based recommendations. Their work ensures that guidelines are scientifically robust and contextually relevant. 23. The WHO Evidence-to-Decision frameworks for screening strategies to prevent early-onset GBS disease in newborns compare universal, risk-based, and combined screening approaches. These frameworks evaluate the impact of screening on maternal and neonatal outcomes, including the incidence of GBS infections, perinatal mortality, and antimicrobial resistance. 24. The WHO prioritizes critical and important outcomes in the development of recommendations for maternal and neonatal health. These outcomes include the incidence of early-onset GBS infections, perinatal mortality, neonatal sepsis, maternal satisfaction with care, and the cost of care.
